newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr rising in late Tokyo after setting new highs.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rising in late Tokyo after setting new highs.

text.p: 0653 GMT 2400 GMT NYK CLOSE
The dollar was rising against the yen in late Tokyo on Monday on a slew of stop-loss buying and investor buying, after hitting a 2-1/2-year high earlier.

Various operators were flocking to snap up dollars after weekend meeting at which Group of Seven (G7) rich nations continued to hail a strong dollar, and on expectations that U.S.-Japan interest rate gap could stay wide, dealers said.
The dollar rose to as high as about 111.50 yen at 0700 GMT.
The greenback earlier hit 111.22 yen in afternoon trade, its highest since trading at 111.75 yen on January 25, 1994.
This year's high of 111.20 yen was set in July 8.
"Since the dollar clearly penetrated 111.20 yen, it is now gathering the momentum to 112 yen," said a U.S. bank dealer.
He said the dollar may have a few hurdles to clear to claw up to 113.50 yen on a medium-term basis.
Expectations that Japanese investors could start buying dollars in relation to their fresh offshore investments in October prompted speculators to jump on dollar buying.
Dealers said dollar buying was likely to have picked up speed again after 3.30 p.m. (0630 GMT), which most Japanese firms consider to be the end of the half-year.
"There was actually Japanese investors buying after 0630 GMT, said one bank dealer in Tokyo.

In the currency options market, a situation in which dollar selling demand outpaces buying is set to be reversed for the first time in nearly a year, said a senior dealer at a European bank in Tokyo. He said operators were now mainly buying short-dated dollar call options with strikes at 112 or 113 yen or some even at 115 yen.

Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Sunday in Washington at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund: "Long-term interest rates have previously reflected expectations of stronger economic prospects but some changes have been seen recently, in accordance with conditions."

This pushed down the yield of the bellwether 182nd Japanese government bond (JGB). The United States refrained from raising its key interest rates at last week's policy-setting meeting but many traders still see a chance for the United States to tighten in November.
Japan's closely watched industrial production data for August showed a month-on-month fall of 1.9 percent. Dealers said the weak figure was within market forecasts.

The prospect of continued low Japan's interest rates also encouraged traders to sell the yen against other major currencies. "There's been a fair bit of cross buying, especially in mark/yen and Swiss/yen. Apparently the Japanese investors need to get in some yen crosses for the new Japanese financial half-year," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.
